selected.name: Clear Depiction of Stakeholder Conflict or Tension
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the text highlights a clear, specific conflict between the organization and an identifiable antagonist; score 0 if it presents a sanitized, conflict-free narrative.
selected.rationale: Dense models heavily weight clear adversarial tension or investigative drama (R09, R55), which scorecards miss, instead over-crediting sanitized, generic conflict-free narratives (R03, R06).
member_names: Adversarial Engagement with Named External Party
Clear Depiction of Stakeholder Conflict or Tension
Named adversary with contested facts stated on the record

selected.name: Public-facing stakes
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the described change bears directly on public safety, markets, infrastructure, regulation, consumers, or communities beyond the issuer's insiders; score 0 when it mainly concerns internal culture, branding, routine merchandising, or employee perks.
selected.rationale: R25 concerns consumer data for up to 70 million people and R36 concerns national fuel prices, whereas R16 and R04 primarily describe internal employee benefits.
member_names: Breadth of directly affected general public
General-public stake versus narrow professional-specialty relevance

selected.name: Quantitative Head-to-Head Competitive Benchmark
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the release provides specific numerical comparisons against named competitors, industry averages, or alternative technologies. Score 0 if the release makes only self-referential claims with no external comparison.
selected.rationale: R18 compares fire rates (1 per 100M miles for Tesla vs. 1 per 20M miles for gasoline cars) and combustion energy (10% of a comparable gasoline tank); R16 compares Tesla's TRIR to both the industry average and the prior NUMMI operator. These comparisons give journalists ready-made story angles the scorecard may not detect.
member_names: Comparative Benchmarking Together With Quantitative Evidence
Numeric claim anchored to a named comparison benchmark

selected.name: Named Individuals Performing Specific Actions
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the release names specific individuals and describes concrete, distinctive actions they personally took (not merely their title or a generic quote). Score 0 if all people mentioned are identified only by title and contribute only generic statements.
selected.rationale: R05 identifies RGJ employees whose Jeep had RGJ decals, describes the driver reversing into a Tesla employee, and names the arresting agency; R06/R44 describes Jerome Guillen creating an entire General Assembly line 'in a matter of weeks' and Kevin Kassekert turning 'a pile of rocks in the Sierra Nevada mountains into a factory employing 12 thousand people.' R43 names employees but only in anodyne testimonial quotes ('Knowing Target provides backup care gives our family such peace of mind'). Named human agency drives news interest.

selected.name: Tangible Public Calls to Action Together With Exact Logistics
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the text provides concrete dates, exact pricing, or specific URLs for the public to act immediately; score 0 if it contains vague future promises with no actionable details.
selected.rationale: Dense models favor releases that give consumers immediate, actionable logistics (R21, R38), whereas scorecards over-credit releases lacking any immediate public action (R10, R25).
member_names: Tangible Public Calls to Action Together With Exact Logistics

selected.name: Accountable disclosure
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the issuer acknowledges uncertainty, criticism, failure, or competing claims and supplies specific facts, safeguards, or explanatory detail; score 0 when the text is entirely self-congratulatory and avoids adverse information.
selected.rationale: R12 addresses allegations and missing factual details, R31 apologises for communication with hosts while specifying support measures, and R55 reports both safety improvements and remaining weaknesses.
member_names: Disclosure that cuts against the issuer's own interest

selected.name: Editorially usable completeness
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the text independently supplies a clear subject, actors, timing, location or scope, concrete particulars, and a concise central proposition; score 0 when it is mostly promotional filler, fragmented content, or lacks an identifiable announcement.
selected.rationale: R25 and R50 provide self-contained facts, dates, actors, and practical particulars, while R45 lacks an identifiable release body and R27 offers little beyond a celebratory claim.
member_names: Complete self-contained text a reporter could file from

selected.name: Distinctive Executive Voice with Personality
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the release features a strong, recognisable individual voice using idiosyncratic language, informal phrasing, or personal asides that signal authentic authorship. Score 0 if all quoted or narrative language is corporate-generic and could have been written by any PR department.
selected.rationale: R06/R44 includes 'That is insanely badass' and an informal product-teasing 'And that's just what people know about...'; R18 is signed simply '--Elon' and uses direct, punchy technical prose. R49 is a generic CEO letter full of phrases like 'intrinsically linked to the health and vitality'—no personality at all.
member_names: Direct Executive Voice and Unconventional Phrasing

selected.name: Independent evidentiary grounding
selected.instruction: Score 10 when important claims are supported by named external data sources, independent institutions, multiple attributable parties, or clearly described evidence; score 0 when claims rely only on the issuer's assertions.
selected.rationale: R33 includes statements from three organisations, R37 cites the Case-Shiller index and long historical series, and R39 identifies China's customs authority and its conversion method.

selected.name: Vivid safety or security event
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the release gives a specific incident, causal sequence, and concrete threat to people, property, or public security; score 0 when safety language is generic or hypothetical.
selected.rationale: R24 details injuries and vehicle movements, R33 describes 180 passengers passing without passport checks, and R51 explains a vehicle fire after a severe roadway collision.

selected.name: Primary-source artifact released with the announcement
selected.instruction: Score whether the item hands over primary material rather than only summarising it. 10 = the text reproduces or releases something a reporter can quote and inspect directly - a verbatim internal email or letter, reproduced correspondence with a named third party, downloadable specification or design files, the full underlying data series, a filed document. 5 = extensive verbatim quotation from a single named principal, but no artifact. 0 = nothing but the issuer's own summarising prose, optionally with a marketing link.
selected.rationale: R02 and its repeat R37 are the internal email itself, reproduced verbatim including its asides; R58 reprints the vehicle owner's own correspondence with permission; R26 makes the design and specification files available for download and says so; R14, R19 and R44 point to the whole underlying series. All are dense_high_card_low, several at the top of the slice. An artifact converts a release from a claim into evidence, which is precisely what determines whether an independent outlet can write from it without depending on the issuer; a criterion bank scoring the prose has no reason to notice that the prose is not the payload.
member_names: Primary-source artifact released with the announcement

selected.name: Factual Refutation of External Allegations
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the text directly, point-by-point refutes a specific external accusation, lawsuit, or crisis with hard data; score 0 if it ignores the issue or relies purely on generic apologies.
selected.rationale: Dense models assign high value to fact-based pushback against controversies (R09, R52), while scorecards miss this and over-credit boilerplate crisis responses that lack substantive defense (R03, R06).
member_names: Explicit rebuttal of a named external accuser

selected.name: Industry Structural Change Scope
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the announced change alters how an entire industry operates—a new standard, a cross-platform collaboration, or a move that forces competitors to respond. Score 0 if the announcement affects only the issuing company's internal operations or product line.
selected.rationale: R54 opens Tesla's charging connector to all manufacturers and renames it the North American Charging Standard—a potential industry-wide shift; R13 announces the first cross-platform collaboration between Airbnb and Vrbo on shared safety enforcement. R56 announces a vendor alliance that changes nothing structurally, yet the scorecard rates both similarly.

selected.name: Industry-wide interoperability
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the announcement changes how multiple independent organisations, platforms, or systems can interoperate; score 0 when the change applies only within the issuing organisation.
selected.rationale: R15 opens Tesla's connector design to manufacturers and networks, R58 creates cross-platform information sharing, and R47 combines Airbnb, UNESCO, and a city government.

selected.name: Consequences land on identified parties outside the organisation
selected.instruction: Score who is actually changed by the action, and how wide that set is. 10 = the described action alters something concrete for people outside the issuing organisation - every customer of a product, an entire industry's equipment choices, competitors, regulators, investors - and the text makes clear who they are and roughly how many. 5 = external parties are affected but marginally, or only a small named set. 0 = nothing changes for anyone outside the organisation; the item concerns the issuer's own employees, offices, internal processes, culture or self-image only. Rhetorical invocation of 'communities' or 'the world' with no external change scores 0.
selected.rationale: Contrast R26 (invites every charging network operator and vehicle manufacturer to adopt the connector, and publishes the files that let them) and R24 (every prospective buyer's price, ordering route and feature set changes today) with R39 (an on-site childcare centre for 116 children of the issuer's own employees at one building), R45 (internal guidelines for reopening the issuer's own offices) and R25 (the issuer's own conference moves online). The dense_low_card_high half is dominated by internally-directed acts described in the warm, stakeholder-centred language a criterion bank is built to reward; the axis it misses is simply whether anyone outside the building is affected.
member_names: Consequences land on identified parties outside the organisation

selected.name: Defensive Legal Posturing
selected.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text is structured as a defensive rebuttal to a lawsuit, accident, or regulatory action, using combative language against external critics. Judge the extent of the defensive posture only; do not judge whether the defense is justified.
selected.rationale: R22 ('petition is completely false') and R25 ('appears focused on alleged misconduct') are highly defensive legal rebuttals. Their combative, urgent tone strongly correlates with journalistic coverage (making them newsworthy to the dense model), but they may lack the standard positive PR structure the scorecard expects.
member_names: Defensive posture toward a named external actor or incident
Reactive crisis management and defensive stance
upstream_parent_all_members: submission timing under reactive/defensive pressure (crisis-response cadence)
whether an external event, adversary or regulatory action forced the communication (crisis-response trigger) rather than the organisation choosing its own moment

selected.name: Encoding or extraction damage
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text contains malformed characters, missing spaces, broken markup, HTML artifacts, or visibly corrupted extraction; do not judge whether the feature is good or newsworthy.
selected.rationale: Technical corruption can affect model perception while saying nothing about journalistic value. Examples include the malformed punctuation and spacing in R26 and R32, and the damaged presentation in R42 and R33.
member_names: Scraped web page and CMS navigation artifacts
upstream_parent_all_members: web scraping or CMS export process

selected.name: Formal wire-service dateline/distribution convention
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text opens with formal wire-service dateline conventions: an ALL-CAPS city name followed by a date, an explicit wire-service credit (e.g. '/PRNewswire/'), or a colon-terminated dateline preceding the lead sentence, as opposed to an undated first-person 'company blog' opening. Score only the presence of this dateline/distribution formatting. Do not judge whether the story behind it is important.
selected.rationale: R15 opens with a full wire-service dateline and explicit credit ('TEANECK, N.J. and LONDON, Oct. 4, 2012 / PRNewswire / --') and R49 opens 'MINNEAPOLIS - January 10, 2014'; R03/R19/R28 all open 'NEW YORK, [DATE]:' in the same wire convention. Paid-newswire distribution may correlate with genuinely larger corporate events, so this format marker is plausibly mixed.
selected.upstream_parent: distribution tier / paid newswire vs owned-channel publishing practice
upstream_parent_all_members: distribution tier / paid newswire vs owned-channel publishing practice

selected.name: Consumer purchase-mechanics and promotional offer density
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text is built around consumer-facing purchase mechanics. Count: named shelf or booking prices a shopper would pay; percentage-off, spend-and-save or dollar-off offer structures; promotional windows and shop-by or on-sale dates; gift-card, coupon, cleanse-price, limit-per-customer or cannot-be-combined terms; availability and where-to-look tips; second-person urging to shop, book, check a store or hurry; exclamation-marked enthusiasm about a deal. 0 = no purchase-mechanics material at all. 5 = a section of the text is offer mechanics, the rest is not. 10 = the text is essentially a shopping offer from start to finish. Score ONLY how much of this material is present. You must NOT judge whether the offer is attractive, well written, generous or worthwhile.
selected.rationale: MODE 1 surface, with an honest upstream parent. R06 is a spend-and-save offer with two dated windows and a combination restriction; R33 is a stock-availability tip sheet with a $59.99 price, a two-per-guest limit and dated drops; R36 lists price bands from $1.25 to $49.99 plus product counts; R52 sets a $421 rate and a 10:00 AM PT booking time; R01 wraps a giving milestone in the same shop-friendly voice. Offer-mechanics density identifies the desk that produced the item, which is exactly the sort of provenance a text model can latch onto. Tagged mixed because the producing desk plausibly also bears on genuine news value, so this must appear in the sensitivity band rather than being discounted outright.
member_names: Consumer purchase-mechanics and promotional offer density
selected.upstream_parent: which internal function produced the item (a merchandising/consumer-marketing desk versus a corporate communications, policy or investor-relations desk)
upstream_parent_all_members: which internal function produced the item (a merchandising/consumer-marketing desk versus a corporate communications, policy or investor-relations desk)

selected.name: Corpus Duplication / Repetition
selected.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text appears to be a verbatim duplicate or heavily syndicated copy of another release in the exact same format, lacking any original phrasing for its specific issuance. Judge the extent of the formulaic duplication only; do not judge the quality of the content.
selected.rationale: R31, R41, and R48 are completely identical Target data breach letters. R05 and R60 are identical Tesla emails. A model may score the exact same text multiple times in completely opposite ways depending on the presence of other surface features, creating artificial extremes in the disagreement pool.

selected.name: Named-individual personal-voice signature on the document
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text is voiced as a personal communication from a named individual rather than as an impersonal organisational statement. Count: first-person-singular pronouns ('I', 'me', 'my'); a salutation opening ('Dear ...'); autobiographical framing of the writer's own tenure, role, career length or feelings; an explicit frame stating that the passage is an email, letter or message from a named person; a closing signature giving a personal name, often with a job title; direct expressions of personal thanks, apology or pride in the first person singular. 0 = no personal-voice markers anywhere; the text speaks only as an organisation or in the third person. 10 = the entire text is a signed first-person letter or message. Score ONLY how much personal-voice marking is visible. You must NOT judge whether the personal voice is sincere, appropriate, effective or well executed, and you must not treat a senior-sounding title as evidence of anything.
selected.rationale: MODE 2 upstream-factor. The unseen factor is authorship and seniority; its textual fingerprint is the signature apparatus. R03 opens 'Dear Host' and is explicitly framed as an email from a named co-founder; R08 is a first-person account by a newly hired safety head ('When I recently joined Tesla'); R10 closes with a named chairman and CEO; R16, R44 and R58 are signed guest letters; R27 signs off '-- Elon'; R30 and R47 are framed as an email just sent to employees. The judge scores only the visible signature apparatus, never the unobservable seniority. Tagged mixed because a personally signed item may genuinely mark an occasion the organisation considers weighty.
member_names: Named-individual personal-voice signature on the document
selected.upstream_parent: who inside the organisation drafted and put their name to the item (a named senior executive writing personally versus an unnamed communications team)
upstream_parent_all_members: author's seniority and personal practice of signing communications
who inside the organisation drafted and put their name to the item (a named senior executive writing personally versus an unnamed communications team)

selected.name: Internal Comm Repackaging
selected.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text explicitly frames itself as a leaked or shared internal message directed at a specific internal audience (e.g., using phrases like 'The following email was sent to employees...', 'Dear Host', or 'Dear Target Guest'). Judge the extent of this framing only; do not judge whether it is good or bad.
selected.rationale: Items like R05 and R09 are framed as internal letters ('The following email was just sent to Tesla employees', 'Below is an email... sent to Airbnb hosts'). R31, R41, and R48 are addressed directly to 'Dear Target Guest'. This format signals a dedicated, pre-existing audience and often generates high engagement, skewing dense model perceptions regardless of broad newsworthiness.
member_names: Internal memo or open letter framing
selected.upstream_parent: PR strategy / bypassing wires to use owned audience
upstream_parent_all_members: PR strategy / bypassing wires to use owned audience
intended for an internal or closed stakeholder audience

selected.name: Extent of departure from templated corporate register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the writing departs, in manner alone, from standard corporate-communications register. Count or estimate the presence and density of stylistic departure markers: humour or satire; informal or conversational syntax; first- or second-person address; sentence fragments, dashes, ellipses, all-caps or exclamation marks used for effect; abrupt or one-word closings; self-referential or meta asides; distinctive rhythm or repetition used as a device; slang, profanity or invented coinages; and, on the other side, the ABSENCE of template furniture such as benefit-laden subheads, 'About [Organisation]' boilerplate, and stock phrases ('is pleased to announce', 'end-to-end solution', 'reflects our commitment'). 10 = the manner is thoroughly non-standard throughout -- multiple departure markers in most paragraphs and essentially no template furniture. 5 = ordinary house style with a handful of lines written in a non-standard manner. 0 = uniformly standard corporate register, template furniture intact, no departure markers at all. This is NOT a quality judgement: do not decide whether the departures are effective, charming, appropriate, or embarrassing, do not consider whether the writing is good, and do not consider what the item is about or whether it says anything of substance. A text with the markers and no content whatsoever must be able to score 10; a text full of content and written in flat house style must score 0.
selected.rationale: This is the pure carrier: the observable stylistic fingerprint of a comms function that writes unlike a template, with every trace of merit removed by forbidding any judgement of effectiveness or of content. Dissociation A (high surface, low real): the meme-inflected, one-word-sign-off post that says nothing beyond generic excitement scores 10 here and 0 on the candidate-real component. Dissociation B (low surface, high real): the boilerplate-register release admitting a nine-month slip, its named cause, and the units affected scores 0 here and 10 on the candidate-real component. Because the two are scored on disjoint evidence -- manner versus what is disclosed -- neither direction is blocked.
selected.parent: Distinctive quotable voice rather than interchangeable corporate template
member_names: Extent of departure from templated corporate register
selected.upstream_parent: surface carrier of bank criterion: Distinctive quotable voice rather than interchangeable corporate template

selected.name: Extent of newswire dateline, ticker and boilerplate formatting
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the item is dressed in paid-financial-newswire formatting conventions. Count which of these are present, and how canonically: (a) a capitalized CITY, STATE or CITY, COUNTRY dateline at the head; (b) a date line adjoining it; (c) an explicit wire-service name or branding (e.g. 'PRNewswire', 'Business Wire', 'GlobeNewswire'); (d) a stock ticker in parentheses (e.g. '(NYSE: CRM)', '(Nasdaq: XXXX)'); (e) a 'today announced' or 'today unveiled' construction in the opening sentence; (f) an 'About [Organisation]' boilerplate block; (g) a formal media- or investor-contact block with a name, email or phone; (h) a forward-looking-statements or safe-harbour paragraph; (i) a terminal end mark such as ### or -30-. 10 = essentially all of these present in canonical form. 5 = roughly half present, or several present in loose form. 0 = none present -- the item opens like a blog post, newsletter or social caption with no dateline, wire branding, ticker or boilerplate furniture. Score only the extent of the formatting. This is NOT a quality judgement: do not decide whether the formal presentation is appropriate, professional, or makes the underlying matter more or less important, and do not consider what the item says.
selected.rationale: This is the distribution-tier fingerprint on its own -- a countable inventory of format furniture, with merit removed because the judge is barred from weighing content or from treating formality as a virtue. Dissociation A (high surface, low real): the fully wire-formatted brand-refresh release with no date, quantity or named outside party scores 10 here and 0 on the candidate-real component. Dissociation B (low surface, high real): the undressed blog post giving the closure date, the 620 positions and the state filing scores 0 here and 10 on the candidate-real component. The counting instruction is mechanical, so an item with every marker and no substance reaches 10 unimpeded.
selected.parent: Formal wire-service dateline and ticker format
member_names: Extent of newswire dateline, ticker and boilerplate formatting
selected.upstream_parent: surface carrier of bank criterion: Formal wire-service dateline and ticker format

selected.name: Extent of un-recapped prior-installment presupposition
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text requires the reader to already know about an earlier, un-recapped announcement from this organisation on this topic. Count or estimate: explicit back-references ('update on', 'further to', 'as previously announced', 'as we said in', 'following our earlier'); continuity framing ('the ongoing', 'continues to', 'phase two', 'the next step in', 'despite extensions on previous deadlines', 'was uncovered as part of the ongoing'); definite descriptions of programmes, products, investigations, agreements or deadlines that the text names as already known and never introduces or explains; unexplained internal shorthand, version numbers or programme codes; and, conversely, the absence of first-time-reader scaffolding (who the organisation is, what the topic is, what happened before). 10 = the text is heavily anaphoric throughout and a first-time reader could not reconstruct the prior installment from anything in it. 5 = some back-reference, but the prior context is largely recoverable from the text. 0 = fully self-contained: everything is introduced from scratch, with no reliance on an un-recapped earlier announcement. Score only the extent of the presupposition. This is NOT a quality judgement: do not decide whether presupposing prior knowledge is good or bad writing, and do not consider whether whatever is being updated is significant or whether anything has actually changed.
selected.rationale: This is the pure positional fingerprint of being a later item in a run -- countable anaphora and missing scaffolding -- with merit stripped out by forbidding any judgement of significance or of whether the situation has moved. Dissociation A (high surface, low real): the 'further to our previous update on the ongoing initiative' item that recaps nothing and reports no movement scores 10 here and 0 on the candidate-real component. Dissociation B (low surface, high real): the fully self-contained item explaining the recall from scratch while reporting the jump from 400 to 12,300 units and the new deadline scores 0 here and 10 on the candidate-real component. Because scoring rests on textual back-reference alone, an item saturated with continuity markers and empty of any development reaches 10.
selected.parent: Presupposes an earlier installment in series
selected.upstream_parent: surface carrier of bank criterion: Presupposes an earlier installment in series

A.rule: FREEZE DECLARATION identity rule -- concept identity by full-recall blind pairwise adjudication, never embedding-tau. The cosine only shortlisted candidate pairs (cross-proposer pairs at cos >= 0.55).

strict_merge_output.note: Track-A strict two-judge merge written as a NEW file so the cited tau-era species file is not moved. The tau-only figures are preserved here under the *_PREMERGE_tau_only keys.
